ito-guide--communications-antenna.mu.content:
>Positioning a radio antenna
A clear, safely positioned antenna can improve a link; test both directions.

Keep antennas upright if that is how they are designed and the other station is similarly polarised. An unobstructed position, or greater safe height, may help reduce the effect of buildings and terrain. Trees and wet materials can also weaken a signal. Move a portable radio a short distance and test again.
Keep antenna cables as short as practical and use suitable connectors. Turn the transmitter off before disconnecting an antenna. Never install an antenna near overhead power lines; do not climb a roof or tree during bad weather. Use qualified help for permanent outdoor installations, earthing and lightning protection.
Antenna gain and cable loss affect radiated power. Make sure the complete installation meets the applicable legal limits.

ito-guide--communications-emergency.mu.content:
>Getting emergency help
For immediate danger call 999 or 112 and ask for the emergency service you need.

Give your location, what happened, people involved and a number for a return call. Follow the call handler’s instructions. In the hills or mountains ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue; at the coast ask for Coastguard.
A mobile 999 or 112 call can use another available UK network if your own has no coverage. Some phones offer emergency satellite contact where supported; it depends on the device, service and conditions. Emergency SMS requires registration in advance: text register to 999 and follow the reply. It still needs a mobile network.
A Reticulum or LoRa message does not directly reach 999 unless a specific service has confirmed it can receive and relay it. Do not assume anyone is monitoring.

ito-guide--communications-licensing.mu.content:
>UK radio rules
Before transmitting, check the conditions that apply to your exact equipment, frequency and use.

Licence-exempt does not mean unrestricted. UK short-range radio rules can specify frequency ranges, radiated power, antenna and airtime limits. Conditions vary by sub-band and may change. Check current Ofcom requirements and the equipment instructions; transmitter power alone is not the same as radiated power.
PMR446 handheld radios have their own equipment and use rules. Shared channels are not private or protected from interference. An amateur radio licence has separate conditions; do not assume it authorises encrypted Reticulum traffic. Ofcom’s amateur guidance restricts encrypted messages between amateur stations, with specified exceptions.
This page is a starting point, not a full licence. Follow the relevant current licence or exemption for your installation.

ito-guide--communications-lora.mu.content:
>LoRa basics
LoRa is a low-power radio method; compatible settings and software are needed at both ends.

LoRa can carry small amounts of data over long distances in suitable conditions, but buildings, terrain, trees, interference and antenna placement change the result. Radio bandwidth, spreading factor and coding rate affect range and speed. Both ends of a direct link must use compatible radio settings and the same network protocol.
Reticulum can use compatible RNode radios. LoRa alone does not mean that a device supports Reticulum, MeshCore, Meshtastic or LoRaWAN interchangeably. A page transfer can take a long time or fail, especially across several hops.
Shared frequencies have legal operating limits. Do not assume higher power or a larger antenna is permitted.

ito-guide--communications-mesh.mu.content:
>How network relays work
A relay can extend reach only if it is compatible, powered and able to hear both sides.

In a multi-hop network, information may pass through intermediate nodes. Reticulum transport must be enabled on nodes intended to forward traffic. A node within radio range is not automatically a usable relay; settings, paths and network load matter.
Each radio hop uses shared airtime. Weak links, interference or a powered-off relay can delay or stop delivery. A stronger signal from one neighbour does not prove the full path or return path works.
Test messages both ways with a known person before relying on a route. Keep messages short and do not repeatedly flood the channel with retries.

ito-guide--communications-nomad.mu.content:
>Nomad Network basics
Nomad Network lets a node host small pages that other reachable nodes can read.

A host must be powered, have hosting enabled and be reachable over Reticulum. Use the host’s Nomad destination address in a compatible browser. Pages can link to others on the same host or another destination; another host may not be reachable.
Choose short text pages on slow radio. A page that was cached on your device may be available offline, depending on the client and its cache settings; test this before relying on it. A node may be offline, pages may be old, and a destination address does not certify the accuracy of content.
Ito support is under development. The steps and availability in a finished Ito interface have not yet been verified.

ito-guide--communications-offline.mu.content:
>Communicating without internet
Agree a primary and backup method with people before an outage.

A direct radio or local Reticulum path can work without internet if all required devices, compatible links and power are available. A route that normally uses an internet-connected relay will fail if that connection is lost and no other route is available.
Keep written phone numbers, agreed radio settings and destination addresses. Test in both directions with the internet disconnected. Agree check-in times and a meeting place. A battery radio can receive public broadcasts if a local station is operating, but reception is not two-way communication.
For an emergency try 999 or 112 first. A mesh message is not a confirmed emergency-service call; seek another route to help if no acknowledgement arrives.

ito-guide--communications-planning.mu.content:
>Emergency communications plan
Write down who to contact, how to reach them and what to do if there is no reply.

Choose a primary and backup contact method and meeting place. Record telephone numbers, radio channels and settings, Reticulum destination addresses and local contacts on paper. Agree check-in times, who will listen, and who can call 999 if a radio request is received.
Test each route both ways, including with the internet disconnected. Check battery capacity, charging leads and whether any relay needs mains power. Share plans with household members and account for accessibility and medical equipment.
Update the plan when people, addresses or equipment change. Do not assume a mesh, a mobile mast, a cached page or an emergency contact will be available.

ito-guide--communications-power.mu.content:
>Conserving radio power
Plan for the whole system: radio, host, network equipment and charging losses.

Charge batteries and power banks before bad weather. Keep compatible charging leads and, where suitable, a spare charged battery. Use a tested power source that matches the device’s voltage, polarity and current requirements. Keep batteries dry and protect them from damage and extreme temperatures.
Use short messages and avoid unnecessary repeated announcements, large downloads and automatic retransfers. Lower screen brightness or switch off unused accessories. Agree check-in times before switching equipment off; a sleeping or unpowered node cannot receive messages or relay for others.
Do not disconnect a node that others rely on without coordinating. Keep a separate way to contact emergency services.

ito-guide--communications-radio.mu.content:
>Using a radio to request help
Use an authorised radio and a channel where someone has agreed to listen.

Speak slowly and briefly. Say who you are, your location, the emergency, number of people, immediate dangers and what help is needed. Ask the listener to repeat the location and confirm whether they are contacting emergency services. Wait for a reply; do not assume a transmission was heard.
If using a handheld radio, allow a moment after pressing transmit before speaking, then release the button to listen. Avoid interrupting urgent traffic. An ordinary shared radio channel has no guarantee of monitoring, privacy or delivery.
Call 999 or 112 directly if possible. Radio equipment and channels are subject to UK licence or exemption conditions; know them before using the equipment.

ito-guide--communications-reticulum.mu.content:
>Reticulum basics
Reticulum is a networking system that can operate over several kinds of connection.

Devices use destinations to address services or people. Nodes announce destinations and, where configured as transport nodes, can forward traffic over available interfaces. A path may include more than one hop. Reticulum can use radio, local networks or internet links; a route is not guaranteed to exist.
Links encrypt data between endpoints, but this does not prove that the person or information at the other end is trustworthy. Verify identities and destination addresses in advance. Keep a backup of your identity using the application’s instructions and protect it from others.
An internet outage does not disable a purely local radio path, but devices, power, compatible settings and a reachable peer are still needed.

ito-guide--communications-signal.mu.content:
>Understanding radio signal
A received signal reading is a clue, not a delivery guarantee.

RSSI describes received signal strength, commonly in dBm: a value closer to zero is stronger, so -90 dBm is stronger than -110 dBm. SNR compares signal with noise; a larger value generally means more margin above noise. Some LoRa signals can be decoded at negative SNR, depending on settings and conditions.
Readings usually describe what your device received, not what the other person received. Different transmit power, antennas, obstructions and interference can make the two directions perform differently. Multi-hop readings may describe only part of the route.
Compare repeated tests with the same settings and a known peer. A successful reply or delivery acknowledgement is more useful than a single signal reading.

ito-guide--first-aid-adult-cpr.mu.content:
>Adult CPR and defibrillator
Unresponsive and not breathing normally, or only gasping: call 999 and start CPR.

1. Put the phone on speaker. Ask someone to bring an AED (defibrillator) if available; do not leave the person to fetch one if alone.
2. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top. With straight arms, push down 5 to 6 cm, 100 to 120 times a minute. Let the chest rise fully after each push.
3. Continue compressions. If trained and willing to give breaths, use 30 compressions then 2 breaths. Follow the call handler’s instructions.
4. Switch on the AED as soon as it arrives, attach pads to the bare chest and follow its voice prompts. Keep clear when told; resume CPR when instructed.
Continue until the person shows signs of life or a professional takes over. Child and baby CPR differs: see Child CPR.

ito-guide--first-aid-assess.mu.content:
>Assessing an emergency
Make the scene safe. Call 999 or 112 for life-threatening danger.

Do not put yourself in danger. Check for hazards such as traffic, electricity, fire or fumes. Ask a bystander to call for an ambulance and give your location.
Check response: speak loudly and gently shake the shoulders. If unresponsive, call 999 immediately on speaker and open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing.
Not breathing normally: start CPR immediately. If breathing normally but unresponsive, place in the recovery position and keep checking breathing; if spinal injury is suspected, avoid unnecessary movement and follow the call handler’s advice. Control severe bleeding with firm pressure.

ito-guide--first-aid-bleeding.mu.content:
>Severe bleeding
Press firmly on the wound immediately and call 999.

1. Wear gloves if available. Apply firm, continuous direct pressure with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. If nothing is available, use your hand or ask the person to press.
2. If an object is embedded, leave it in place and press firmly on either side; do not press on the object. Cover around it.
3. Have the person lie down if possible and keep them warm. Keep pressing and follow the call handler’s instructions. Watch for worsening response or breathing.
If the dressing becomes soaked, apply another on top and keep pressure on. Do not delay pressure while looking for supplies. A tourniquet may be needed for catastrophic limb bleeding when direct pressure fails; follow emergency service instructions.

ito-guide--first-aid-burns.mu.content:
>Burns and scalds
Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes.

Move away from the source if safe. Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn before swelling, but do not remove anything stuck to the skin. Keep the rest of the person warm while cooling the burn. Do not use ice, butter, creams or adhesive dressings.
After cooling, loosely lay clean cling film over the burn; do not wrap it tightly around a limb. A clean clear plastic bag can cover a hand. Do not burst blisters.
Call 999 for serious burns or breathing difficulty. Large or deep burns, white or charred skin, burns to face, hands, feet, joints or genitals, and chemical or electrical burns need urgent hospital assessment. For chemicals, avoid contact and rinse with plenty of running water; follow emergency instructions. Switch electricity off before touching the person.

ito-guide--first-aid-child-cpr.mu.content:
>Child and baby CPR
A child or baby who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs immediate CPR.

Call 999 on speaker and follow the call handler. Gasping is not normal breathing. If possible have someone bring an AED without delaying CPR.
Open the airway and give 5 initial rescue breaths, each about one second, looking for the chest to rise. For a baby, cover both mouth and nose with your mouth. Then give 30 chest compressions followed by 2 breaths, repeating. Push in the centre of the chest to about one third of its depth; use one or two hands for a child, or the two-thumb encircling technique for an infant.
If unable or unwilling to give breaths, give chest compressions. Apply the AED as soon as available; use child pads or child mode if available without delaying treatment. Follow prompts. Continue until help takes over or the child shows signs of life.

ito-guide--first-aid-choking-baby.mu.content:
>Choking: baby under one
Call 999 on speaker and act immediately if the baby cannot cough, cry or breathe effectively.

1. Support the head and place the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest. Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades.
2. If still choking, turn the baby face up on your knees, supporting the head. Give up to 5 sharp chest thrusts in the centre of the chest, using the two-thumb encircling technique.
3. Alternate up to 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts. Stop as soon as the obstruction clears. Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby. Do not sweep blindly inside the mouth; remove an object only if clearly visible.
If the baby becomes unresponsive, start child and baby CPR, beginning with 5 rescue breaths. Follow the call handler. Seek a healthcare assessment after chest thrusts.

ito-guide--first-aid-choking.mu.content:
>Choking: adults and children
Call 999 as soon as you recognise choking; use speaker if alone.

If they can cough effectively, encourage coughing. If they cannot cough effectively, speak or breathe, act immediately.
For adults and children over one: lean them forwards and give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades. If still choking, stand behind, place a fist between the navel and bottom of the breastbone, grasp it and pull sharply inwards and upwards up to 5 times. Alternate 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until clear or unresponsive.
For a pregnant person, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Do not use abdominal thrusts on a baby under one: see Choking baby.
If unresponsive, start CPR. Only remove an object if clearly visible; never sweep blindly. After abdominal or chest thrusts, seek healthcare assessment, even if the person seems well.

>Suspected broken bone
Keep the injured part still and supported. Do not straighten it.

Call 999 for an open fracture, suspected broken long bone, back, neck or pelvis, or a serious incident. Move the person only if necessary for immediate safety.
Support the injured area above and below the injury in the position found; use soft padding. Remove rings or watches from an injured limb before swelling if this can be done without moving it. For an open wound cover with a clean dressing and press around, not on, protruding bone.
Check fingers or toes for numbness or unusual colour or coldness and tell the call handler. Other suspected fractures need urgent assessment at A&E or an urgent treatment centre. Keep the person warm and watch their breathing.

ito-guide--first-aid-heat.mu.content:
>Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
Move the person somewhere cool and start cooling immediately.

Heat exhaustion can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating, weakness and thirst. Lay them down, remove unnecessary clothing, cool the skin with water and fan it. If awake and able to swallow, give cool water or a suitable rehydration drink.
Call 999 immediately for confusion, a seizure, loss of consciousness, shortness of breath or other severe symptoms. Also call if they remain unwell after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids. Heatstroke can be life-threatening.
While waiting, keep cooling with a cool wet sheet, water and fanning. Do not give an unresponsive person a drink. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR.

ito-guide--first-aid-hypothermia.mu.content:
>Hypothermia first aid
Suspected hypothermia is a medical emergency: call 999.

Signs can include shivering, pale cold skin, slurred speech, slow breathing, confusion or drowsiness. Move the person gently to shelter if safe. Remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground and wrap in dry blankets, covering the head. Stay with them and monitor breathing.
If fully awake and able to swallow, offer a warm non-alcoholic drink and sugary food. Do not give anything by mouth to an unresponsive person.
Do not rub limbs, use a hot bath, heat lamp or hot water bottle, or give alcohol. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and follow the 999 call handler.

ito-guide--first-aid-supplies.mu.content:
>First aid supplies
Keep a first aid kit accessible, dry and easy to take with you.

Include disposable gloves, sterile dressings, assorted plasters, bandages, medical tape, a thermometer, antiseptic, sterile eyewash and tweezers. Keep a written list and emergency phone numbers with it.
Plan for prescribed medicines and equipment your household depends on, such as diabetes supplies. Store medicines safely away from children and follow their storage instructions. Check supplies and expiry dates at least every six months; replace used or damaged sterile items.
A practical first aid course helps you use the kit and respond while emergency help is on its way.

ito-guide--first-aid-wounds.mu.content:
>Cleaning a minor wound
First stop bleeding with direct pressure. Severe or uncontrollable bleeding needs 999.

Wash hands and use gloves if available. Once bleeding has stopped, rinse a minor wound with safe tap or bottled water. Clean the surrounding skin with soap and water, wiping away from the wound. Cover with a sterile dressing or plaster; change it when wet or dirty.
Do not remove an embedded object. Get urgent medical advice for bites, a wound still dirty after cleaning, spreading redness, swelling, increasing pain or pus. A tetanus injection may be needed. Deep or large wounds, loss of feeling or movement, or an embedded object need urgent assessment.

ito-guide--food-cooking.mu.content:
>Cooking without mains power
Use food that needs no cooking when safe cooking or water is unavailable.

An outdoor camping stove or barbecue can heat food where its use is permitted; follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Never use one indoors, in a tent, garage or other enclosed space: carbon monoxide can kill. Keep it away from tents, dry grass and flammable materials.
Use safe water and clean utensils. Follow food packet instructions; cook food thoroughly and make sure it is steaming hot throughout. Keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food. Wash hands with soap and safe water before preparing food and after handling raw food.
Do not use food touched by floodwater. Plan for safe cooling and refrigeration of leftovers, or prepare only what will be eaten.

ito-guide--food-hygiene.mu.content:
>Preventing food contamination
Wash hands with soap and safe water before handling food and after using the toilet.

Keep raw meat, fish and poultry separate from ready-to-eat foods. Use separate utensils or wash boards and equipment thoroughly in hot soapy water between tasks. Clean surfaces and containers; use safe water for food and cleaning.
Cook food thoroughly and keep chilled food cold. Do not prepare food for others if you have vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not eat food touched by floodwater or use water suspected of chemical contamination.
If safe water is unavailable, use hand sanitiser when handwashing is not possible and obtain a safe water supply as soon as possible.

ito-guide--food-planning.mu.content:
>Planning emergency meals
Choose familiar food that fits the household’s needs and can be prepared safely.

Plan several days of meals and include food that can be eaten cold. Check allergies, baby feeding, medical and cultural needs, pets, utensils and a manual tin opener. Allow safe water for drinking, cooking and washing hands.
A power cut may make refrigeration and cooking unavailable. Use perishable food while it is still safe, then use shelf-stable food. Do not eat food past its use-by date or food that has warmed for too long.
Review the supplies regularly, replace used items and check dates. Keep the plan practical for anyone who may need to use it.

ito-guide--food-power-cut.mu.content:
>Food safety during a power cut
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed; check temperature with a thermometer.

An unopened fridge should stay cold for up to about four hours. A full freezer may keep food frozen for up to 48 hours, or 24 hours if half full; these are estimates, not guarantees. Check temperatures and follow local guidance.
Normally keep the fridge at 5°C or below. If it reaches 8°C or above, food that normally needs refrigeration should be eaten within four hours or discarded, unless power returns within that period. Take extra care with people at higher risk of food poisoning.
Do not rely on smell or taste to prove food is safe. Discard food touched by floodwater. Use camping stoves and barbecues outdoors only.

ito-guide--food-preservation.mu.content:
>Preserving food safely
Use food storage methods and recipes from reliable, tested guidance.

Freezing can preserve food only while it stays frozen. Follow packaging instructions and check dates; mark and rotate stored food. During a power cut, keep freezer doors closed and check its condition when power returns.
Home bottling, canning and foods stored in oil can create conditions for botulism. Do not improvise pressure, acidity, time or temperature, or assume that boiling a sealed jar makes food safe. Garlic or herbs in oil and low-acid vegetables need particular care. If you cannot follow a tested method, use another food source.
Never taste food from a swollen, leaking or otherwise suspect container.

Store foods your household can eat without refrigeration or cooking.

Follow storage and use-by instructions. A use-by date is about safety: do not eat the food after that date even if it looks or smells fine. A best-before date concerns quality. Discard leaking, swollen or damaged containers. Do not taste suspect food.

>Camping stove safety
Use a camping stove outdoors, away from people, tents and flammable materials.

Follow the appliance and fuel manufacturer’s instructions. Place it securely on a stable non-flammable surface; keep children and pets away. Never leave it unattended while lit. Turn it off before moving it and let it cool before changing fuel or packing it away.
Never use it indoors, in a tent, porch, awning or garage. Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless and can kill. Do not bring a barbecue inside even after cooking. If fire spreads, move away and call 999.
Check local wildfire restrictions and campsite rules before lighting any stove.

ito-guide--navigation-compass.mu.content:
>Using a compass
Practise compass use with a map before you need it in poor visibility.

Hold the compass level and keep it away from phones, metal and magnets. For a map bearing, place the compass edge from your known position towards the destination. Turn the housing so its orienting lines align with the map’s north-south grid lines and north points to the top of the map. Read the bearing at the index line.
Account for the current difference between grid north and magnetic north, using the map’s diagram and date. Hold the compass level, turn your body until the magnetic needle aligns with the orienting arrow, and follow the direction-of-travel arrow. Pick safe visible features along the route.
A bearing is not proof that a route is safe: check terrain and practise with an instructor.

ito-guide--navigation-lost.mu.content:
>What to do when lost
Stop in a safe place, stay together and work out your options.

Check the map and compass against your last known position and recognisable features. Do not continue into unknown steep ground, water, cliffs or worsening weather. Shelter from wind and rain and put on dry layers. If anyone is injured, treat immediate dangers.
If you cannot find a safe way out, call 999 or 112 early. In the hills ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue; on the coast ask for Coastguard. Give your best location, number of people and injuries. Follow the operator’s instructions and stay where rescuers expect you unless you must move from danger; inform them if you move.
Conserve phone battery, but remain contactable. Use a whistle or torch if needed.

ito-guide--navigation-maps.mu.content:
>Reading a map
Use the map’s key, scale and contours to understand the ground.

Find the map scale and legend: symbols, paths and access rights vary by map. Orient the map so that north on the page matches the ground, using a compass and identifiable features. Locate yourself using several features, such as a path junction, stream and hill shape; do not rely on a single landmark.
Contour lines join places of equal height. Closely spaced lines indicate steep ground; wide spacing suggests gentler slopes. Read the contour interval in the key and plan around cliffs, streams and difficult terrain.
Carry a suitable paper map and compass and practise before venturing into unfamiliar country.

Choose a route suited to the least experienced person in the group.

Check the forecast, daylight, distance, terrain, access and escape routes before leaving. Carry a paper map and compass, waterproofs, warm layers, food, water, torch, whistle, charged phone and emergency shelter. Know how to use them.
Tell a trusted person your route, expected return time and what to do if you are overdue. Allow extra time for bad weather or difficult terrain. Turn back or change plans if conditions exceed the group’s abilities.
In an emergency in the hills, call 999 or 112, ask for Police and then Mountain Rescue. Give your location and follow their directions.

ito-guide--navigation-signal.mu.content:
>Signalling for help outdoors
Call 999 or 112 first if possible; give your location and stay available.

In the hills or mountains ask for Police and then Mountain Rescue. At the coast ask for Coastguard. If you have already called, follow the rescue team’s instructions and stay in the agreed safe place.
The mountain distress signal is six long whistle blasts or torch flashes in one minute, followed by one minute’s pause; repeat until someone reaches you. Continue after hearing a reply, as rescuers may use the sound to locate you.
Move away from immediate danger, shelter from the weather and keep warm. Do not risk cliffs, rivers or fire to attract attention.

ito-guide--navigation-without-gps.mu.content:
>Navigating without GPS
Use a paper map and compass; confirm your location frequently.

Before leaving, mark the route, known landmarks, escape routes and likely junctions. Orient the map and compare multiple features with the ground. Track your direction, distance and time; check at each junction rather than waiting until you are lost.
Do not navigate by the sun, moss, a single landmark or a guessed path when a mistake could be dangerous. Weather, darkness and unmarked hazards can make a route unsafe. Turn back early if conditions or your abilities make progress uncertain.
If lost, stop in a safe place, shelter and reassess. Seek help early if you cannot safely locate or leave your position.

ito-guide--power-battery-safety.mu.content:
>Charging and storing batteries
Use the manufacturer’s charger or an approved compatible replacement.

Keep batteries and chargers dry, uncovered and away from bedding, heat, combustible materials and escape routes. Follow the manufacturer’s temperature and storage instructions. Do not charge while asleep or away from home. Protect batteries from crushing, puncture or immersion.
If a battery swells, becomes unusually hot, leaks or smells unusual, stop use and disconnect charging if safe. Do not open or repair the pack; contact the manufacturer or a qualified technician. If it starts smoking or catches fire, get out, stay out and call 999. Do not breathe the fumes or attempt to carry a burning battery outside.
Do not put batteries in household rubbish: use an appropriate battery recycling collection.

ito-guide--power-capacity.mu.content:
>Battery capacity and power
Watt-hours describe stored energy; watts describe the rate at which a device uses it.

A battery rated 500 Wh stores up to about 500 watt-hours when full. A 10 W load running for 10 hours uses about 100 Wh. Estimate energy by multiplying watts by hours, and add the needs of all devices. Manufacturers’ capacity is not all available at the socket: conversion losses, the battery condition and cut-off limits reduce usable energy.
Watts also matter: a unit may have enough stored energy but be unable to supply a high-power appliance. Motors can need a higher starting surge. Check continuous output, starting limits and compatibility; never assume a pump will start from its running watts alone.
Milliamp-hours alone are not comparable across different voltages: Wh = mAh × volts ÷ 1,000.

ito-guide--power-electrical.mu.content:
>Electrical danger during an outage
Keep clear of fallen power lines: assume they are live.

Do not touch a cable or anything in contact with it. Keep others away and report it to the electricity network operator on 105 in Great Britain. Call 999 for immediate danger or if a road or path is blocked.
Never touch electrical equipment with wet hands or while standing in water. Do not use damaged cables, overloaded sockets or improvised adapters. Keep power stations and electrical connections dry. If someone receives an electric shock, do not touch them until the power is safely isolated; call 999.
Never backfeed household wiring from a generator, battery or vehicle through a socket. Have a qualified electrician design and install any household backup connection and protective isolation.

ito-guide--power-generator.mu.content:
>Using a fuel generator safely
Never use a fuel generator indoors, in a garage or in a partially enclosed space.

Run it outdoors at least 6 metres from doors and windows, with the exhaust pointing away. Greater separation or another position may be needed to keep fumes away from buildings and people. A running generator produces deadly, odourless carbon monoxide; an open garage door or fan does not make indoor use safe. Fit working CO alarms in the home.
Keep the generator dry and follow its operating instructions. Stop it and let it cool before refuelling; store fuel safely away from heat. Use equipment and leads rated for the load.
Never plug its output into a wall socket or improvise a connection to household wiring. A qualified electrician must design and install a suitable changeover and isolation arrangement.

ito-guide--power-loads.mu.content:
>Prioritising electrical loads
List essential loads and estimate both their energy use and peak power.

Start with medically necessary equipment and its agreed backup plan, then communication, lighting, essential water and food storage. Record each device’s watts, hours per day, connector and any starting surge. Add watts for things running together and watt-hours over the period they are needed.
Switch off non-essential loads and use a torch instead of lighting whole rooms. A heater, kettle or cooker can use a large amount of energy quickly. Fridges and pumps may cycle automatically and draw a high starting surge: test compatibility, not just the stated running wattage.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed and follow food safety guidance. Reserve enough power for urgent communication.

ito-guide--power-medical.mu.content:
>Power for medical equipment
If loss of power puts someone in immediate danger, call 999.

Before an outage, discuss a written backup and escalation plan with the person’s clinical team and equipment provider. Identify the correct backup supply, how long it lasts, any alarms or switching delay, safe storage of medicines and when to seek help. Test only as directed by the provider.
Ask the electricity supplier and network operator about the Priority Services Register and tell them about electricity-dependent equipment. Registration provides extra support but does not guarantee uninterrupted electricity or immediate restoration.
Keep the provider’s emergency number, contacts and plan on paper. Battery or power-station output compatibility, capacity and changeover must be confirmed for the specific equipment; do not assume a generic unit is suitable.

Keep a torch, charged phone, power bank and written emergency numbers within reach.

In Great Britain call 105 to report a power cut or contact your electricity network operator. For immediate danger call 999. Keep battery lights, a radio, water, ready-to-eat food and essential supplies available. Know how to release any electrically operated gates safely.
If someone depends on powered medical equipment or telecare, agree a tested backup plan with their healthcare or equipment provider. Ask your electricity supplier and network operator about their Priority Services Registers; registration is support, not a guaranteed power supply.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed. Never use a barbecue, camping stove or fuel generator indoors, in a garage or tent: carbon monoxide can kill.

>Estimating battery runtime
Estimate runtime using usable watt-hours divided by the device’s average watts.

Example: if a battery can deliver 400 Wh at its output and a device averages 20 W, the ideal estimate is 400 ÷ 20 = 20 hours. Actual runtime can be shorter because of inverter overhead, changing loads, cold, battery age or automatic shutdown. The usable figure may be much lower than the advertised battery capacity; measure it with the real setup.
Include all loads, such as the router, radio and host computer. A fridge or pump cycles and may need a large starting surge; its label alone does not establish average consumption or successful start-up.
Leave a reserve and test safely before an outage. Do not rely on estimates for life-support equipment.

ito-guide--power-solar-home.mu.content:
>Home solar during a power cut
Do not assume rooftop solar will power your home when the grid fails.

Many grid-connected solar systems shut down during a power cut for safety. A suitable inverter and properly configured backup or island-mode installation are needed for the circuits intended to operate independently. A battery alone does not guarantee backup capability or an uninterrupted changeover.
Check your own system’s documentation and ask its installer which sockets or circuits remain powered, how switching works, what it can start and whether solar can recharge the battery during an outage. Test in advance with qualified guidance.
Never alter wiring, bypass protective equipment or feed a generator or power station into a wall socket. Household backup and grid isolation require a qualified electrician.

ito-guide--power-solar-portable.mu.content:
>Charging from portable solar
Match the panel and connector to the power station’s specified solar input.

Before connecting, check the unit’s permitted input voltage, current, polarity and connector. The panel or connected array’s open-circuit voltage must remain below the station’s maximum, including in cold conditions; series wiring raises voltage. Follow both manufacturers’ instructions. Do not improvise wiring or exceed stated limits.
Actual output depends on sun, cloud, shade, angle and temperature; a panel’s rated watts are not a guarantee of continuous charging. Place the panel securely where it cannot overheat or obstruct people, and keep the power station and non-weatherproof connections dry and out of direct heat.
Plan for poor sunlight and test the whole system beforehand.

ito-guide--power-station.mu.content:
>Using a portable power station
Check the output is suitable before connecting an appliance.

Use the manufacturer’s specified voltage, current, connector and output type. Add the watts of appliances running at the same time and stay within the station’s continuous rating. Starting a motor, pump or compressor can need more power than its running rating. Confirm surge support and test the actual appliance.
Keep the unit dry, uncovered and ventilated, and within its permitted temperature range. Charge with an approved charger; stop using a damaged, swollen or unusually hot battery. Follow the manufacturer’s guidance on unattended use and storage.
Never feed a portable station into a household wall socket. Household backup circuits require a properly designed installation by a qualified electrician.

ito-guide--preparedness-evacuation.mu.content:
>Emergency evacuation
Leave promptly when instructed or when staying places you in immediate danger.

Take medicines, essential medical equipment, phone, charger, keys, identification, warm clothing, drinking water and supplies for children and pets if time allows. Tell someone where you are going. Follow the emergency services’ route and instructions.
If leaving due to flooding, turn off gas, electricity and water only if safe and instructed. Never walk or drive through floodwater. Do not touch electrical equipment while standing in water.
Keep a grab bag and a written list of essential contacts. Do not return until authorities say it is safe.

ito-guide--preparedness-flood.mu.content:
>Preparing for flooding
If in immediate danger call 999. Never walk or drive through floodwater.

Before flooding, prepare medicines, a torch, phone charger, waterproof clothing, essential documents and a way to leave. Move valuables and medicines upstairs if safe. Follow local warnings and evacuation instructions.
If leaving and only if safe, turn off gas, electricity and water. Do not touch electrical equipment while standing in water. Floodwater can contain sewage and chemicals; avoid contact and use a safe water supply.
If trapped, move to a higher safe place and call 999. Do not enter a loft without an escape route.

>Household emergency kit
Keep essential supplies together where everyone can find them.

Include safe drinking water, ready-to-eat food and a manual tin opener, torch, spare batteries, battery or wind-up radio, power bank, first aid supplies, hygiene items and essential medicines.
Plan at least 3 litres of drinking water per person per day; allow more for cooking, hygiene and individual needs. Include baby supplies, mobility or medical equipment, pet food, warm clothing and copies of important numbers.
Check expiry dates and equipment every six months. Do not rely on one phone or mains-powered connection.

Agree how to contact each other and where to meet.

Write important phone numbers on paper. Decide a nearby and an out-of-area meeting point, and an alternative if phones fail. Identify safe routes out and keep keys accessible.
Know how to turn off water, gas and electricity if instructed and safe to do so. Record medicines, equipment and support needs. Check neighbours who may need help, with their consent.

ito-guide--preparedness-power-cut.mu.content:
>During a power cut
Check whether neighbours are affected and report the fault.

In Great Britain call 105 to report a power cut or get information from the electricity network operator. For immediate danger call 999. Keep a torch and charged power bank available.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed. Switch off or unplug sensitive equipment if safe. Check on people who rely on powered medical devices or telecare; follow their established backup plan and contact their provider.
Never use a barbecue, generator or camping stove indoors or in an enclosed space: carbon monoxide can kill. Landlines and mobile networks may also fail during prolonged outages.

ito-guide--preparedness-sanitation.mu.content:
>Emergency sanitation
If water or sewage services fail, follow the water company and local authority instructions.

Keep drinking water separate from water used for flushing. If the sewer system is working and local advice permits, non-drinking water can be used for flushing. If told not to flush because sewage services have failed, do not flush.
For a national outage, UK public health guidance advises collecting faeces in plastic bags, sealing them and placing them in an outside household waste bin; follow any different local disposal instructions. Keep waste away from food, children, animals and water sources.
Wash hands with soap and safe water after using the toilet and before food preparation. Use sanitiser if handwashing is unavailable. Avoid contact with sewage and floodwater.

ito-guide--preparedness-storm.mu.content:
>Preparing for a severe storm
Check warnings, secure loose items before weather worsens and stay away from hazards.

Charge phones and power banks; prepare torches, a battery radio, drinking water and medicines. Secure garden furniture and other loose objects if safe. Avoid unnecessary travel during severe conditions and follow local instructions.
Keep away from fallen power lines and anything touching them; assume they are live. Report a power cut or dangerous electricity equipment on 105 in Great Britain, and call 999 for immediate danger. Never use generators or camping stoves indoors.
Check on neighbours who may need support, if safe to do so. If told to evacuate, follow the emergency services’ directions.

>Growing basic food crops
Start with a few crops your household eats and a sunny, accessible growing space.

Lettuce, chard, herbs and beans can be grown in suitable beds or containers; follow the seed packet for sowing times, spacing and care. Use containers with drainage and appropriate peat-free compost. Containers dry out more quickly than garden soil, so check them regularly and water when needed.
Keep food-growing areas clear of floodwater and other contamination. Wash harvested produce with safe water. Allow for weather, pests and growing time: a small garden supplements stored food and is not a reliable immediate emergency supply.

Protect drinking water first; use separate non-drinking water where appropriate.

Reserve safe water for drinking, food preparation, handwashing and necessary medical needs. Fix leaks when safe and practical. Use a bowl for washing and turn taps off while soaping. Follow your supplier’s instructions during an outage.
Collect rainwater in a covered, labelled butt for watering plants or flushing only when the sewer system is working and local advice permits. Do not drink water-butt water. Water plants at the roots and check containers regularly; use mulch where suitable to reduce drying.

ito-guide--shelter-alarms.mu.content:
>Smoke, heat and CO alarms
Working alarms give early warning. Test them regularly and keep exits clear.

Fit smoke alarms in rooms where a fire may start, except the kitchen, where a heat alarm is more suitable. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for location, testing, maintenance and replacement. Never remove batteries to silence an alarm without restoring protection.
Fit an audible carbon monoxide alarm in each room containing an appliance burning gas, oil, coal or wood. A carbon monoxide alarm is not a smoke alarm. Maintain appliances, chimneys and ventilation; an alarm does not replace maintenance.
Make and practise an escape plan, including help for anyone who cannot escape unaided. Ask your local fire and rescue service for tailored home safety advice.

ito-guide--shelter-camping.mu.content:
>Tent and camping fire safety
Keep stoves, heaters, barbecues and flames out of tents and enclosed shelters.

Fuel-burning equipment can cause fire and deadly carbon monoxide, even where you cannot smell smoke. A barbecue can remain dangerous after cooking: never bring it inside to cool or warm a shelter. Use a battery torch rather than a candle.
Cook outside, away from tent walls, long grass and other flammable material. Follow appliance and campsite instructions. Store fuel and gas cylinders outside the tent, away from heat, and keep children away.
Know the campsite emergency arrangements and how to escape the tent. If fire spreads, get everyone away and call 999. If clothes catch fire: stop, drop and roll.

ito-guide--shelter-carbon-monoxide.mu.content:
>Carbon monoxide poisoning
If you suspect carbon monoxide, get outside into fresh air immediately.

Stop using the suspected appliance if you can do so safely. Do not go back inside until advised it is safe. Carbon monoxide has no smell or colour. Headache, dizziness, nausea and weakness can be signs; symptoms may improve outside or affect several people.
Call 999 if an exposed person has difficulty breathing, confusion, loss of consciousness, weakness, chest pain or muscle pain. For other suspected symptoms, call NHS 111 promptly. If you suspect a gas appliance is leaking carbon monoxide, call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999.
Never use a barbecue, camping stove or generator indoors, in a tent or garage. Fit an audible carbon monoxide alarm in each room containing a fuel-burning appliance, and maintain appliances and flues.

ito-guide--shelter-emergency.mu.content:
>Emergency outdoor shelter
Get out of immediate danger, protect the group from wind and rain, and call for help early.

In the hills or mountains, call 999 or 112, ask for Police and then Mountain Rescue. Give your location, injuries, number of people and phone number. At the coast ask for the Coastguard. Follow the operator’s instructions.
Use a group shelter, bivvy bag or emergency blanket if available. Choose a place away from hazards such as steep ground, falling rocks and rising water. Insulate the person from the ground and add dry layers. Do not waste time searching for distant shelter if conditions make travel unsafe.
After calling for rescue, stay where the team expects you unless you must move from danger; tell rescuers if you move. Never use a stove or flame inside a tent or enclosed shelter.

ito-guide--shelter-heat-prevention.mu.content:
>Staying safe in extreme heat
Move to a cooler place, drink regularly and watch for signs of heat illness.

Close curtains or blinds against direct sun. If it is hotter outside, close windows during the day and ventilate when it is cooler and safe to do so. Wear loose light clothing, rest in the shade and avoid strenuous activity in the hottest part of the day. Never leave children or animals in a parked car.
Check on people at higher risk, including older people, young children and people with long-term illness. Follow individual medical advice about fluid restrictions.
Confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures or breathing difficulty in a hot person needs 999. Start cooling immediately. If the person remains unwell after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids, call 999.

ito-guide--shelter-house-fire.mu.content:
>Fire in your home
Warn others. If you can escape safely, get out, stay out and call 999.

Do not stop for belongings or try to fight the fire. Close doors behind you if possible. Use stairs, not lifts. In smoke, keep low. Before opening a door, check it with the back of your hand; do not open it if warm.
If you cannot escape safely, go to a room as far from fire and smoke as possible, close the door, block gaps with soft material, call 999 and tell the operator where you are. Go to a window if safe and follow their instructions.
For a fire elsewhere in a purpose-built block, follow your building’s evacuation plan and fire service instructions. If fire, smoke or heat affects your flat, leave if safe. Never re-enter a burning building.

ito-guide--shelter-insulation.mu.content:
>Keeping heat in safely
Reduce draughts and use dry layers, while keeping essential ventilation clear.

Close curtains at dusk and internal doors to keep warmth in occupied rooms. Use draught excluders at doors and wear several light layers. Sit on a cushion or folded blanket rather than directly on a cold floor, and use dry bedding.
Do not block fixed air vents, chimneys or flues: fuel-burning appliances need ventilation and can produce carbon monoxide. Keep fabric and bedding away from heaters and open fires. Maintain a clear escape route.
If the house cannot be kept safely warm, seek help and a warmer place. Confusion, drowsiness or slurred speech in a cold person needs urgent action: call 999 for suspected hypothermia.

ito-guide--shelter-outdoor-fire.mu.content:
>Lighting a fire outdoors
Avoid lighting a fire when there is wildfire risk or local rules prohibit it.

A cold meal and extra layers are safer choices when conditions are dry or windy. Check site rules and local restrictions. Use a fire only where permitted, on a suitable non-flammable surface, well away from tents, buildings, vegetation and other combustible materials.
Keep water or sand nearby and never leave a fire unattended. Do not use petrol or paraffin to light solid fuel. Keep children and pets away. Put the fire completely out and ensure ashes are cold before leaving or disposing of them.
Never take a fire, barbecue or camping stove into a tent or enclosed shelter. If fire spreads, move away and call 999; do not attempt to tackle it.

ito-guide--shelter-prevent-cold.mu.content:
>Preventing hypothermia
Cold, wind and wet clothes can cause dangerous heat loss, even above freezing.

Wear warm layers with windproof and waterproof outer clothing. Carry a hat, gloves, spare dry layers and an emergency shelter. Eat and drink regularly. Take extra care with children, older people and anyone who is ill or exhausted.
If someone is getting cold, stop, find shelter from wind and rain, replace wet clothing with dry layers and insulate them from the ground. Do not let tiredness or worsening weather leave you far from safety.
Shivering, slurred speech, confusion or drowsiness may indicate hypothermia. Call 999 and use the hypothermia first aid page.

ito-guide--shelter-warm-home.mu.content:
>Staying warm without heating
Keep dry, wear layers and seek help before a home becomes dangerously cold.

Choose one room to spend time in; close internal doors and curtains. Wear several loose, dry layers, warm socks and a hat. Use blankets and insulate yourself from cold floors. Eat regularly and have warm drinks if available.
Check on people who may struggle to keep warm, especially older people, babies and those with health conditions. If safe warmth is unavailable, seek a warm place and ask family, neighbours or your local council for help.
Never use a barbecue, camping stove or generator indoors, in a tent or garage. They can produce deadly carbon monoxide. Call 999 for suspected hypothermia.

ito-guide--shelter-wildfire.mu.content:
>Wildfire safety
If you see an uncontrolled outdoor fire, move away and call 999.

Give the fire service your location and follow its advice. Do not approach the fire, attempt to fight a spreading fire or put yourself in danger to collect belongings. Warn others as you move to safety if you can do so safely.
In dry or windy conditions, avoid lighting fires. Use barbecues only where permitted in designated areas and follow local restrictions. Dispose of cigarettes safely and never discard hot ashes.
Follow evacuation instructions promptly. Routes can become dangerous as wind and smoke change; follow the emergency services rather than relying on a fixed escape direction.

ito-guide--water-boiling.mu.content:
>Boiling water
Boiling kills disease-causing germs; it does not remove chemical pollution.

1. If cloudy, let sediment settle and pour off clear water, or filter through a clean cloth. This step does not make water safe by itself.
2. Bring water to a rolling boil for one minute. Above 2,000 metres, boil for three minutes.
3. Let it cool naturally. Store covered in a clean, sanitised food-grade container.
Use a safe stove outdoors when required by its instructions. Never run a camping stove indoors. If fuel or chemicals are suspected, use another source.

ito-guide--water-dehydration.mu.content:
>Recognising dehydration
Offer safe fluids early if the person is awake and able to swallow.

Signs include thirst, dry mouth, dark urine, passing less urine, tiredness and dizziness. Give small frequent sips if feeling sick. For vomiting or diarrhoea, a pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration solution.
Call 999 for dehydration with confusion, difficulty waking, breathing difficulty, or pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin. Contact NHS 111 urgently for persistent dizziness on standing, unusual tiredness, fast breathing or heart rate, or much less urine.
Babies, children and older adults are more vulnerable. Ask 111 for advice about a child under five.

ito-guide--water-disinfection.mu.content:
>Chemical disinfection
Use only a product labelled for drinking water and follow its instructions.

First let cloudy water settle and pour off clear water, or filter it through a clean cloth. Use the amount and contact time on the product for that volume and temperature. Keep the water covered while it stands.
Some disinfectants do not reliably kill parasites such as Cryptosporidium; boiling is preferable. People who are pregnant, have thyroid problems or are sensitive to iodine should avoid iodine-treated water.
Do not guess a bleach dose: products vary. Disinfection does not remove fuel or toxic chemicals. Find a different source if these are suspected.

ito-guide--water-filtration.mu.content:
>Water filters and their limits
A clear-looking drink can still be unsafe.

A clean cloth or coffee filter removes particles, not reliably germs. A purpose-made filter only removes what its specification says. Many portable filters do not remove viruses or dissolved chemicals.
Check the manufacturer’s instructions, maintenance and freezing limits. Unless the product specifically treats the relevant risks, boil the filtered water or use an appropriate additional disinfection method.
Boiling and most filters do not make water containing fuel or toxic chemicals safe. Use another source.

ito-guide--water-rainwater.mu.content:
>Collecting rainwater
Rainwater from a roof or water butt is not safe to drink untreated.

Collect in a covered, clearly labelled container for flushing or other non-drinking uses. Keep it separate from the drinking-water system; do not connect it to household plumbing without suitable approved protection.
Roofing, droppings, debris and stored water can contaminate it. Prefer a confirmed safe drinking-water source. Boiling can kill germs but cannot remove chemical contamination; use a different source if pollution is suspected. Do not drink floodwater.

ito-guide--water-safe-water.mu.content:
>Making water safe
Use a known safe supply first. Follow the water supplier’s notice.

1. Use sealed bottled water or water confirmed safe by the supplier. Use it for drinking, brushing teeth, food and baby formula.
2. If germs are suspected, boil clear water at a rolling boil for one minute; let it cool in a covered container. Above 2,000 m, boil for three minutes.
3. If boiling is impossible, use drinking-water disinfection tablets exactly as labelled. They may not kill every parasite.
Fuel, chemicals and radioactive material are not removed by boiling or ordinary disinfectant. Use a different safe source. Do not drink floodwater.

ito-guide--water-sources.mu.content:
>Finding emergency water
Use water from a confirmed safe source.

Check local supplier instructions and emergency bottled-water distribution. Sealed commercially bottled water is preferable. Water already stored in clean food-grade containers may be usable if protected from contamination.
If the only source is untreated surface water, choose the clearest water away from pollution and treat it before use. Clear water can still contain germs. Do not use water suspected of containing fuel, chemicals or radioactive material: boiling does not remove them.
Never drink water from heating radiators or boilers. Do not use floodwater.

ito-guide--water-storage.mu.content:
>Storing drinking water
Store safe drinking water in clean, food-grade containers with tight lids.

Wash and sanitise containers before filling, following suitable product instructions. Never reuse containers that held fuel, pesticides or other toxic chemicals. Label drinking water with the date; keep it cool, out of sunlight and away from chemicals.
Replace home-stored water every six months. Pour rather than touching the water or container opening. Keep a separate clearly labelled supply for washing and flushing.
Plan for at least 3 litres per person per day for drinking; allow more for heat, washing, cooking, illness, babies and pets.
